\title{Does Epidemic Physics Help a Graph Network Forecast Dengue? A Leakage-Controlled Test Against Persistence}

% TODO(authors): decision D1 still has placeholders. VENUE: [VENUE]. PAGE LIMIT: [6 + references / 6 including references].
\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{[NAMES, AFFILIATION, EMAILS]}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Graph neural networks and epidemic (SEIR) models are proposed to improve weekly district-level dengue forecasts.
We test these ideas under a protocol that forbids future information and always reports a persistence baseline, which repeats last week's count.
On a rebuilt series for 25 Sri Lankan districts, last week's cases explain 89\% of the variance in this week's cases, and the best climate variable explains 3\%. % EV-004
Over nine rolling forecast origins, persistence has a test RMSE of 28.54 cases per district-week, and no learned model is significantly better (smallest adjusted $p$ is 0.576; the best gap is 1.1 cases). % EV-100, EV-113, EV-114, EV-150
Selection on validation can mislead: one model reaches an adjusted $p$ of 0.023 on validation and 0.694 on test. % EV-108
An SEIR output head that learns its force of infection from scratch is 12.2 cases worse than persistence. % EV-109
On validation, the repair of three failing encoders by a gated SEIR head is explained by its persistence anchor and not by the epidemic equations, although the SEIR version is lower on test. % EV-037, EV-159, EV-160, EV-161
A learned adjacency, GAN and simulator augmentation, longer climate lags and COVID-19 policy covariates gave no measurable test gain.
A 95\% interval built from past persistence residuals covers 96.0\% of targets with a mean width of 99 cases, narrower than every Gaussian-head interval we tested (123 to 250 cases; legacy-array folds). % EV-142, EV-144, EV-145, EV-146, EV-147, EV-148
We recommend that dengue forecasting studies report persistence at every horizon, use paired tests over many forecast origins, and show test results next to validation results.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
dengue forecasting, graph neural networks, persistence baseline, physics-informed learning, rolling-origin evaluation, SEIR model
\end{IEEEkeywords}

%=====================================================================
\section{Introduction}
Dengue is a mosquito-borne disease that causes recurring epidemics in Sri Lanka~\cite{tissera2020severe}.
Forecasts of weekly cases for each district, a few weeks ahead, could help health officers decide where to place clinical capacity and vector control.
Graph neural networks model exchange between neighboring districts, and epidemic compartment models encode how infection spreads.
Several papers combine the two~\cite{weng2024graph,gulmohamed2026denguegnn,rodriguez2023einns,wang2022causalgnn,cao2023mepognn,liu2025seirlstm}.

A forecast is useful only if it beats a trivial baseline.
For weekly counts, the trivial baseline is persistence: repeat last week's value.
On our data, last week's count explains 89\% of the variance in this week's count. % EV-004
The benchmark paper for this dataset reports no persistence baseline~\cite{weng2024graph}.
On that paper's protocol and the same test slices, persistence scores an RMSE of 34.67, while our reproduction of its STGAT model~\cite{huang2019stgat} scores 42.31. % EV-089
Two further problems make published gains hard to read.
The widely used data array contains one week that is wrong because of a formula error in the source table, and persistence scores 44.80 with that week and 29.52 without it. % EV-006
Studies with few forecast origins also cannot produce small $p$-values: an exact sign-flip test on three origins cannot return $p$ below 0.25. % EV-181

We therefore ask a narrow question.
We test which additions help weekly district-level forecasting under a protocol with no future information, persistence reported at every horizon, and paired tests over nine forecast origins.
Our contributions are as follows.
\begin{enumerate}
\item A leakage-controlled rolling-origin protocol with persistence at every horizon, causal input lags, and paired tests over nine origins (Sections~\ref{sec:data} and~\ref{sec:setup}).
\item A measurement of how one mis-computed week changes the persistence baseline, and of how a small number of origins limits testing (Sections~\ref{sec:data} and~\ref{sec:results}).
\item A controlled comparison of output heads. On validation, the gain of a gated SEIR head over failing encoders is explained by its persistence anchor, although on test the SEIR version is lower. A bare SEIR head with a population-scaled force of infection on an adaptive graph is 1.26 cases worse than persistence, and the effect of the scaling alone is untested for the bare head (Section~\ref{sec:results}). % EV-111
\item Negative results for four common additions, each tested against its own control: a learned adjacency, generated training data, climate lags and policy covariates, and spatial priors (Section~\ref{sec:results}).
\end{enumerate}

%=====================================================================
\section{Related Work}
Weng et al.~\cite{weng2024graph} benchmark five spatio-temporal graph networks, STGAT, A3T-GCN, ASTGCN, DCRNN and AAGCN, on weekly Sri Lankan dengue counts~\cite{huang2019stgat,guo2019astgcn,bai2021a3tgcn,shi2019aagcn,li2018dcrnn}.
Their comparison set has no naive baseline.
DengueGNN~\cite{gulmohamed2026denguegnn} builds a dynamic adjacency from an assumed gravity-mobility law and adds no mechanistic constraint.
Graph WaveNet~\cite{wu2019graphwavenet} supplies the adaptive adjacency that we reuse.

Several epidemic models place mechanistic structure inside a neural network.
Liu et al.~\cite{liu2025seirlstm} let an LSTM output the force of infection of an SEIR model for Sri Lankan dengue, which is the design our SEIR heads follow with graph encoders.
EINNs~\cite{rodriguez2023einns}, CausalGNN~\cite{wang2022causalgnn} and MepoGNN~\cite{cao2023mepognn} add epidemiological structure to graph or recurrent models.
We use a human-only SEIR model, as Liu et al. do, although host-vector SEIR-SEI models are common for dengue~\cite{phaijoo2018sensitivity}.
Physics-informed losses~\cite{raissi2019pinn} can fail to train when the constraint is hard to satisfy~\cite{krishnapriyan2021failure}.

For small data sets, TimeGAN~\cite{yoon2019timegan} generates synthetic series.
We test it, a simulator-based variant, reversible instance normalization~\cite{kim2022revin} and district embeddings~\cite{shao2022stid} as additions to our best model.
For uncertainty, likelihood-based forecasters~\cite{salinas2020deepar} produce predictive distributions, and interval scores are best judged together with width~\cite{bracher2021evaluating}.

\section{Data and Problem Setup}\label{sec:data}
We forecast weekly dengue notifications for the 25 districts of Sri Lanka.
We rebuilt the series from the original weekly epidemiological reports.
The rebuilt series has 559 weeks, of which 7 have no report; we leave them missing and never interpolate. % EV-163
Any forecast window that touches a missing week is dropped.
Fig.~\ref{fig:data}b shows the national series, including the large epidemic of 2017~\cite{tissera2020severe}.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_data.pdf}
\caption{National weekly dengue cases (sum over 25 districts). (a) The legacy benchmark array, with the mis-computed week 395 marked. (b) The rebuilt series used in all main experiments.}
\label{fig:data}
\end{figure}

An earlier benchmark array, which we call the legacy array, has 459 weeks~\cite{weng2024graph}. % EV-002
In it, the national total is 7165 cases in week 395, against 396 and 414 in the weeks on either side (Fig.~\ref{fig:data}a). % EV-162
The jump is not a real surge.
The published table for that week (Volume 48, No.~2) has a spreadsheet formula error: 15 of the 24 inner cells of the weekly row equal the sum of the two cells before them, while the table's year-to-date row, which equals the weekly count in the first week of the year, sums, with the Kalmunai division, to 351, which is the published national total. % EV-192
Persistence has an RMSE of 44.80 on the legacy array and 29.52 once that week is excluded. % EV-006
We use the legacy array only in Section~\ref{sec:results} to label older results.

Weekly counts are strongly autocorrelated.
On the rebuilt series, cases in the previous week explain 89\% of the variance of cases in the current week, and the best climate variable explains 3\% (squared correlations 0.8893 and 0.0291). % EV-004
Climate inputs are lagged two weeks and case inputs one week, so a forecast issued at the start of week $i$ uses only reports published before week $i$; a test perturbs every later value and checks that the output does not change. % EV-003
The nine-origin arms use only past cases. % EV-179

The task is to map 3 weeks of counts for all districts to the next 3 weeks, which gives horizons $h=1,2,3$. % EV-007
Districts are nodes of a graph, and two nodes share an edge when the districts share a border.
The graph has 25 nodes and 141 directed edges including self-loops. % EV-010

%=====================================================================
\section{Methods}\label{sec:methods}
Fig.~\ref{fig:arch} summarizes the models.
Every model has a graph encoder that turns the input window into a representation per district, a read-out that gives one value $r_{i,h}$ per district $i$ and horizon $h$, and an output head that turns $r$ into a forecast.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.95\columnwidth]{figures/fig_arch.pdf}
\caption{Model overview. The head either uses the read-out $r$ directly, blends it with the persistence anchor $p$, or sends it through an SEIR simulator whose output is blended with $p$ by a learned gate.}
\label{fig:arch}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Inputs and encoders}
We work with log counts standardized on the training weeks only,
\begin{equation}
z_{i,t}=\frac{\log(1+c_{i,t})-\mu}{\sigma},
\label{eq:z}
\end{equation}
% seirgnn2/core.py::build_tensors (z), build_folds (mu, sigma from training weeks)
where $c_{i,t}$ is the count in district $i$ and week $t$, and $\mu,\sigma$ are the mean and standard deviation of $\log(1+c)$ over the training weeks.
The persistence anchor $p_{i,h}$ is the standardized last observed week, repeated over the horizon.

Our own graph encoder projects the input window to 64 dimensions and applies two message-passing layers with a residual connection around each, % EV-177
\begin{equation}
H^{(l+1)}=H^{(l)}+\mathrm{Dropout}\!\left(\mathrm{ReLU}\!\left(A\,H^{(l)}W^{(l)}\right)\right).
\label{eq:layer}
\end{equation}
% seirgnn2/models.py::GraphLayer.forward, Net.encode
Here $A$ mixes each district with its neighbors.
For the GCN encoder $A$ is the row-normalized border adjacency with self-loops. % EV-183
For the adaptive encoder it is learned,
\begin{equation}
A_{\mathrm{ad}}=\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\mathrm{ReLU}\!\left(E_1E_2^{\top}\right)\right),
\label{eq:adaptive}
\end{equation}
% seirgnn2/models.py::learned_adjacency
with node embeddings $E_1,E_2\in\mathbb{R}^{25\times 10}$ drawn from a standard normal distribution, shared by both layers and exempt from weight decay. % EV-177
A small initialization gives an almost uniform $A_{\mathrm{ad}}$, which is plain averaging over all districts, and weight decay pulls the embeddings back toward it; we therefore use the standard-normal draw and the exemption, and we did not ablate the exemption alone. % EV-050
We also use five published encoders, STGAT, A3T-GCN, ASTGCN, AAGCN and DCRNN, transcribed from the reference code and checked against it, and Liu et al.'s LSTM~\cite{weng2024graph,liu2025seirlstm}.
Our STGAT is the dengue adaptation in that code, a graph-attention layer followed by two LSTM layers, and not the original pedestrian model~\cite{huang2019stgat}.
They replace the graph layers and output a 64-dimensional representation per district.

\subsection{Output heads}
Let $r$ be a linear read-out of the representation.
The five heads are
\begin{equation}
\hat z=\begin{cases}
r & \text{direct}\\
p+r & \text{residual}\\
p+\sigma(a)\,(r-p) & \text{gated}\\
z(\hat c) & \text{SEIR}\\
p+\sigma(a)\,\bigl(z(\hat c)-p\bigr) & \text{gated SEIR}
\end{cases}
\label{eq:heads}
\end{equation}
% seirgnn2/models.py::Net.forward (direct, residual, gated, foi, foi_res)
where $a$ is a learned scalar initialized at $-2$ so that the gate starts mostly closed, % EV-178
and $z(\hat c)$ standardizes the SEIR count forecast $\hat c$ with Eq.~\eqref{eq:z}.

\subsection{SEIR decoder}
For each district the decoder tracks the susceptible, exposed, infectious and recovered fractions $(S,E,I,R)$.
It steps one day at a time with exponential flows, using a force of infection $\lambda_{i,h}$ that is constant within forecast week $h$,
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
f_S&=S\,(1-e^{-\lambda\Delta t}), & S&\leftarrow S-f_S,\\
f_E&=E\,(1-e^{-\omega\Delta t}), & E&\leftarrow E+f_S-f_E,\\
f_I&=I\,(1-e^{-\gamma\Delta t}), & I&\leftarrow I+f_E-f_I,
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:seir}
\end{equation}
% analysis/lib/seir_sim.py::_step, simulate_weeks (R <- R + f_I)
with $\Delta t$ of one day, $\omega=0.7/7$ and $\gamma=1/7$ per day, and 7 steps per week. % EV-011
The weekly count forecast is $\hat c_{i,h}=\rho N_i\sum_{d=1}^{7}f_E^{(d)}$, where $N_i$ is the district population and $\rho=1/11$ is the reporting fraction. % EV-011
% seirgnn2/models.py::Net._physics (counts = inc * rho * pop)
The initial state comes from the last two reported weeks, with the infectious fraction set from $c_{t-1}/(\rho N_i)$ and the exposed fraction from $c_{t-2}/(\rho N_i)$. % EV-170
The susceptible fraction starts from a fixed value and falls with cumulative reported cases.
The exposed fraction and the reporting fraction each carry one learned multiplier; for one variant the exposed multiplier is a function of the district encoding. % EV-173

We test two ways to form the force of infection from the read-out $r$.
The free rate sets $\lambda=\exp(r+b)$ with a learned bias $b$ and an upper clamp. % EV-171
The free rate must therefore learn an offset of about $-\log(\rho N_i S)$ for each district, although it never sees population or $S$.
The anchored rate supplies that scale,
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\hat\lambda_i&=\frac{\max\!\left(c_{i,t-1},\,0.5\right)}{7\,\rho\,N_i\,S_i},\\
\lambda_{i,h}&=\hat\lambda_i\exp\!\bigl(\mathrm{clip}(r_{i,h},-10,10)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:anchor}
\end{equation}
% seirgnn2/models.py::Net._physics, lam_param == "anchor", l.351-358
The first term is the constant daily rate whose seven days of infections, reported at fraction $\rho$, add up to last week's count, and the second lets the network scale it up or down. % EV-172
At $r=0$ the SEIR forecast is close to last week's count but not equal to it, because the simulator does not start in equilibrium, and $S_i$ is the susceptible fraction at the start of the window.

\subsection{Loss, likelihood and training}
The default loss is squared error between $\hat z$ and the standardized target.
Squared error on log counts targets the conditional median, whereas RMSE on counts rewards the conditional mean.
The negative-binomial variant avoids this mismatch by treating the forecast as the mean $\mu$ of a negative-binomial distribution,
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NB}}=-\frac{1}{M}\sum\Bigl[\log\tfrac{\Gamma(y+r_0)}{\Gamma(r_0)\Gamma(y+1)}+r_0\log\tfrac{r_0}{r_0+\mu}+y\log\tfrac{\mu}{r_0+\mu}\Bigr],
\label{eq:nb}
\end{equation}
% analysis/lib/count_loss.py::nb_nll; seirgnn2/train.py::_loss (mu = expm1 of the standardized-scale forecast, r_0 = 1/alpha)
where $y$ is the observed count, $r_0=1/\alpha$ with a dispersion $\alpha$ predicted by the network and bounded above, and $M$ is the number of district-weeks. % EV-176

All models use Adam with a learning rate of 3e-3 and weight decay of 1e-4, batches of 32, cosine learning-rate decay, gradient clipping at 5, and 300 epochs (400 with the NB loss). % EV-175
Early stopping watches validation RMSE in counts with a patience of 40 epochs and restores the best weights. % EV-175
Model B is the AAGCN encoder with a direct head, the NB loss and four seasonal Fourier features of the day of year. % EV-180
All other arms use past cases only. % EV-179

\section{Experimental Setup}\label{sec:setup}
\subsection{Rolling-origin evaluation}
We use rolling-origin cross-validation: we train on all weeks before a cut-off date, test on the weeks after it, then move the cut-off forward and repeat.
For an origin $o$, the cut-off is at a fraction $o$ of all forecast windows.
The 30 windows before the cut-off are the validation set, and the next block of windows is the test set. % EV-182
Standardization uses training weeks only, windows are never shuffled, and windows that touch a missing week are removed.
The main protocol has nine origins from 0.50 to 0.90 in steps of 0.05, and each test block is 5\% of the windows. % EV-186, EV-141
We also use a three-origin protocol (0.55, 0.70, 0.85, test blocks of 15\%) for the wider ablation, because it needs fewer runs. % EV-186, EV-141
Every configuration is trained with seeds 0, 1 and 2 at every origin, which gives 27 runs per arm in the main protocol and 9 in the three-origin protocol. % EV-101, EV-116
Table~\ref{tab:protocols} lists the protocols.
The test weeks differ between protocols, so persistence has a different RMSE in each, and we never place numbers from different protocols in one table.

\input{tables/protocols.tex}

\subsection{Baselines, selection and tests}
Persistence is the first baseline, reported at every horizon.
The baseline GNN is a GCN encoder with a residual head on log counts, which predicts a correction to persistence.
It follows the design of our first tuned baseline, which matched persistence where a GCN trained on absolute counts lost to it, and we retrain it here under the new protocol. % EV-191
Models are selected on validation RMSE only, and test RMSE is read afterwards.
We compare each arm with persistence using the exact paired sign-flip test on the nine origin means, with seeds averaged within each origin, and adjust $p$-values over all 30 arms with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. % EV-149
With three origins, the smallest attainable $p$ is 0.25, so three-origin gaps are reported but not tested; with nine origins it is 0.0039. % EV-181
We do not pool seeds as independent evidence, because the three seeds at one origin share the same data.

The 30 arms of the main protocol are 24 arms from a full grid of six encoders (GCN, LSTM, STGAT, A3T-GCN, ASTGCN, AAGCN) and four heads (direct, residual, SEIR with a free rate, gated SEIR with a free rate), and 6 arms chosen by hand. % EV-179
One author chose the six hand-picked arms after the earlier results were known, and they were not registered in advance. % EV-184
They are five adaptive-encoder variants (a residual head, two anchored gated SEIR heads, an anchored bare SEIR head, a mass-action head) and the GCN encoder with the anchored gated head.
We report all of them next to the 24 grid arms and correct over all 30, but their selection is a weakness that we return to in Section~\ref{sec:discussion}.

\section{Results}\label{sec:results}
\subsection{Main results}
\input{tables/main_p9.tex}

Table~\ref{tab:main} compares the arms with persistence on the nine-origin protocol.
No learned arm is significantly better than persistence on test, and eight are significantly worse. % EV-150
The lowest test RMSE is 27.45, against 28.54 for persistence, shared by the two anchored gated SEIR arms with an adaptive graph (adjusted $p$ is 0.576). % EV-100, EV-113, EV-114
The baseline GNN, a GCN with a residual head, scores 28.12, which is 0.42 below persistence (adjusted $p$ of 0.781). % EV-102
At the three horizons it is lower than persistence by 0.23, 0.15 and 0.79 cases. % EV-165
The same encoder with a direct head scores 28.17 (adjusted $p$ of 0.984). % EV-101
The anchored gated SEIR arm with an adaptive graph is lower than persistence by 0.97, 0.85 and 1.41 cases, so the gap grows with the horizon, but it stays small beside a persistence RMSE of 33.26 at $h=3$. % EV-152, EV-100
STGAT with a direct head fails at 44.71. % EV-106


Validation tells a different story.
On validation, seven arms are significantly better than persistence and eight are significantly worse. % EV-149
One of the seven is the adaptive encoder with a residual head, with a validation RMSE of 25.42 against 27.04 for persistence and an adjusted $p$ of 0.023. % EV-108, EV-100
On test the same model scores 27.94 against 28.54, a gap of 0.60 with an adjusted $p$ of 0.694. % EV-108, EV-100
Selecting on validation would have reported a significant gain that the test blocks do not support.

\subsection{The SEIR head and its parameterization}
With a free rate, the bare SEIR head on a GCN scores 40.77, which is 12.23 cases worse than persistence (adjusted $p$ of 0.033). % EV-109
With the anchored rate and an adaptive graph, the bare head scores 29.80, which is 1.26 cases worse and not significant (adjusted $p$ of 0.781). % EV-111
These two arms differ in the graph as well as in the rate, so the change cannot be assigned to the rate alone.
We have no bare-head arm that pairs the two rates on one graph.
For the gated head the pairing exists: on a GCN encoder, the anchored rate gives 27.62 and the free rate gives 28.43, and neither is significantly different from persistence. % EV-112, EV-110

Table~\ref{tab:p3} shows the three-origin ablation, which we read as indicative only.
With three origins no gap can reach $p$ below 0.25. % EV-181
The simple graph control, a GCN with a residual head, scores 34.50 against 36.02 for persistence. % EV-116, EV-115
Removing the graph gives 34.57 and a learned adjacency gives 34.17, so the whole spread across the three graph choices is 0.41 cases, well inside the standard deviation of 10 to 11 over runs. % EV-117, EV-118, EV-116, EV-187
Direct heads fail on two published encoders: STGAT scores 62.00 and DCRNN scores 73.52 against persistence at 36.02. % EV-123, EV-125, EV-115
Their gated SEIR versions score 35.84 and 35.52. % EV-124, EV-126

\input{tables/ablation_p3.tex}

To separate the anchor from the physics, we ran a gated head without the simulator.
On validation, the simulator adds nothing for the three failing encoders: the SEIR head minus the gated head is $+0.66$ (STGAT), $0.00$ (A3T-GCN) and $-0.68$ (DCRNN) in RMSE. % EV-159, EV-160, EV-161
The anchor and gate account for 1.12, 1.00 and 0.96 of the repair. % EV-159, EV-160, EV-161
On test, the SEIR head is lower than the gated head by 0.62, 1.66 and 3.50. % EV-159, EV-160, EV-161
Validation and test disagree.
Because validation is the pre-set criterion, we do not credit the repair to the simulator.

The best three-origin arm is AAGCN with a gated head, at 33.53 against 36.02 for persistence. % EV-120, EV-115
This gap is untested.
The nine-origin protocol contains no gated head without physics, and its ASTGCN arm with a residual head is 0.11 above persistence. % EV-107

Model B, which uses the NB loss and seasonal features, has the lowest validation RMSE in Table~\ref{tab:p3}, 15.51 against 17.86 for persistence. % EV-127, EV-115
On test it scores 37.54, which is above persistence at 36.02. % EV-127, EV-115
Its squared-error twin scores 16.27 on validation and 35.94 on test. % EV-128
The NB loss lowers validation RMSE by 0.76 on all 9 matched runs, but raises test RMSE by 1.61; the matched runs count seeds as independent, so this is a statement about stability and not about the series. % EV-033

Fig.~\ref{fig:valtest} puts all three-origin configurations on one plot.
Of 69 configurations, 56 have a validation RMSE below that of persistence, and 25 of those 56 have a test RMSE above it. % EV-164
Across eight comparison families, the configuration with the lowest validation RMSE is worse than persistence on test in five. % EV-039

\subsection{What did not help}
Table~\ref{tab:neg} lists changes to model B on the three-origin protocol.
TimeGAN augmentation raises test RMSE by 0.52 and SEIR-simulator pre-training by 0.92. % EV-130, EV-131
Climate lags change test RMSE by $+0.51$, $-0.05$ and $-0.47$ for lag ranges of 2 to 4, 2 to 13 and 2 to 25 weeks, and the largest gain wins on 8 of 9 matched runs, but those runs share three origins, so it is not a tested gain. % EV-132, EV-133, EV-134
A spatial penalty on relative incidence changes test RMSE by $-0.02$. % EV-135
The metapopulation SEIR head has the largest test change, $-2.51$ with 6 of 9 runs better, but its validation RMSE is 17.34 against 15.51 for B, and validation and test disagree again. % EV-136, EV-129

\input{tables/negative_p3.tex}

Two more tests used the nine-origin setting of earlier experiment code with cases-only SEIR-STGAT as the control.
Lagged policy and workplace-mobility covariates give test RMSE of 30.06 and 30.07 against 30.05 for the cases-only model, with Holm-adjusted $p$ of 1.0 for both. % EV-068
A movement-restriction prior with fixed exponents of 0.5, 1 and 2 gives 30.59, 31.28 and 32.43 against 30.07, and is significantly worse at the two larger exponents. % EV-069

Older results on the legacy array, which includes the week-395 error, are not comparable with the tables above.
A physics-style spatial loss and an adaptive graph gave a pooled RMSE of 44.64 against 45.47 for the fixed graph and 44.80 for persistence, and a paired $t$-test against the fixed graph gave $p$ of about 0.10 to 0.14. % EV-083
WGAN-GP augmentation raised RMSE on the middle fold to 124.13, against 43.71 with no augmentation and 41.74 with jitter and warping. % EV-086

\subsection{Interval forecasts}
A Gaussian output head gives a predictive interval.
These comparisons use the legacy-array folds, which include the week-395 error, because the Gaussian-head results exist only there.
On those folds, the nominal 95\% intervals of the Gaussian head cover 94.7\% to 96.2\% of targets, with mean widths of 123 to 250 cases. % EV-144, EV-145, EV-146, EV-147, EV-148
A simple interval needs no network: persistence plus the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of training-window residuals, per horizon. % EV-188
It covers 96.0\% of targets with a mean width of 99 cases, and a version scaled by $\sqrt{1+c_{t-1}}$ covers 96.3\% with a mean width of 74 cases. % EV-142, EV-143
The simple intervals are narrower than every Gaussian-head interval at similar coverage.
We therefore do not claim calibration as a contribution of the neural models.


%=====================================================================
\section{Discussion and Limitations}\label{sec:discussion}
\subsection{What we learned}
Persistence is a hard baseline for a reason that the data state plainly.
Last week's count explains 89\% of the variance of this week's count, and climate adds almost nothing at a causal lag. % EV-004
A model has 11\% of the variance left to explain, and a window of three weeks gives it little to explain it with. % EV-004, EV-189
We believe this is why the additional inputs we tried (climate lags, policy covariates, neighbor information through a graph) each left test RMSE within half a case of their control. % EV-132, EV-133, EV-134, EV-068, EV-117, EV-118

The gated SEIR head does help three encoders that fail with a direct head, but on validation the anchor does that work.
A gated head without the simulator repairs them as well, although the SEIR version is lower on test by 0.62 to 3.50. % EV-159, EV-160, EV-161
Physics is not useless here, but we could not show that the epidemic equations add accuracy over a persistence anchor with a learned gate.

Two diagnostics point to likely reasons why the bare SEIR head loses.
First, the free rate has to learn a population-and-susceptible offset it never sees.
Regressing the oracle log force of infection on past cases, log population and log $S$ raises the out-of-sample $r^2$ on reachable cells from 0.35--0.38 to 0.59--0.67 across three origins. % EV-060
Second, 39\% to 41\% of cells are pinned at a force of infection of zero, because the exposed compartment alone already overshoots the target, and no rate can lower the forecast below that floor. % EV-061
The anchored rate addresses the first reason and not the second.

The learned adjacency does move away from uniform: its normalized row entropy is 0.469 on average, against 1.000 for a uniform matrix. % EV-050
Its strongest edges do not follow geography.
Examples are Kalutara from Kandy and Jaffna from Kegalle, which are not neighbors. % EV-185
We believe the graph encodes shared outbreak timing rather than adjacency, but we did not test this, and the encoder gains nothing measurable over no graph on three origins. % EV-117, EV-118, EV-116

The arm with the lowest validation RMSE in Table~\ref{tab:main}, ASTGCN with a residual head at 25.23, is 0.11 above persistence on test, and in five of eight comparison families the validation pick lost to persistence on test. % EV-107, EV-039

\subsection{Limitations}
The nine origins give 9 paired units, which allows $p$ down to 0.0039 but gives low power for differences of one case. % EV-181
Six of the 30 main arms were hand-picked after earlier results, the 46-arm grid planned for them was not run, and the Benjamini-Hochberg family therefore does not describe a clean selection. % EV-184
The static graph in all main runs contains two edges that are not real borders, Kandy to Ampara and Kegalle to Kalutara; a corrected file exists, and we did not repeat the main runs with it. % EV-010
Fixed epidemic constants (reporting fraction, latent and infectious rates) are taken from the literature and not fitted by district. % EV-011
The interval comparison and the older WGAN-GP and adaptive-graph results use the legacy array, which contains the week-395 error.
We study one country, one disease and a horizon of three weeks.

%=====================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
On a leakage-controlled nine-origin protocol, no learned model is significantly better than persistence on test, whose RMSE is 28.54 cases per district-week against a best learned 27.45. % EV-100, EV-114, EV-150
On validation, the gain of an SEIR head over failing encoders is explained by its persistence anchor, although on test the SEIR version is lower, and a validation-selected model reached an adjusted $p$ of 0.023 on validation and 0.694 on test. % EV-037, EV-108
Future dengue forecasting studies should report persistence at every horizon, test with many origins, and show validation and test results together.
